note: X posts for the agentwright-cron worker. Each item is posted once at or after `at` (within 3 hours; later than that it is skipped and reported). The worker runs at :07 every hour, so the real posting time is the first :07 at or after `at` (`at` 02:30 goes out at 03:07). No post may really go out between 03:00 and 07:00 KST, so never set `at` between 02:08 and 06:07 KST; night slots are 23:00, 01:00 and 02:00 KST, one item per slot (two items due in the same hour go out an hour apart). No links unless the item is a click-now item (max 1 link post/day). Edit on main; no redeploy needed. Before merging a change to this file run `npm run check:queues` (real posting times, length limits, links to posts that are not open yet). Optional per item: community_id (numeric X Community id the account has joined; posted with share_with_followers, falls back to a normal post + alert if refused; max 1 community post/day, never the same text in two communities). Top-level "paused": true stops all posting (emergency stop for policy changes).

In a typical Claude Sonnet 5.5 request (4,000 tokens in, 600 out, 60% cached), output is 13% of the tokens and 64% of the cost.

If you want to cut your bill, look at max_tokens and answer length before you look at the prompt.

Claude Fable 5.2 costs $8 in / $40 out per million tokens, 2x Opus 5.5.

4,000 tokens in, 600 out, 60% cached:
Sonnet 5.5: $0.0094
Opus 5.5: $0.0189
Fable 5.2: $0.0373

Cache reads are $0.20/M on both Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, so cache-heavy agents pay less than 2x.

Same request on Claude Sonnet 5.5, 4,000 tokens in and 600 out:

0% cache hits: $0.0140
60% cache hits: $0.0094

One cache_control line on the system prompt. It is the first thing to check before any pricing change.

A $20/month AI plan on Claude Sonnet 5.5, 300 requests per user: 76% margin.

The same user at 10x usage: -52%. Break-even is about 1,900 requests a month.

Run your own numbers in our free margin calculator (link in profile, under Tools).

If you recompute last month's LLM costs with today's price table, your totals move.

Store the rate used on every usage row, version the price table, and keep raw token counts so a re-price is a deliberate step.

Full write-up with code on our blog, link in profile.

Agentwright Starter is on Product Hunt today: a Next.js starter kit for Claude-powered agent SaaS with per-user cost tracking.

If you build on the Claude API, we'd like to hear what a kit like this is still missing.

https://www.producthunt.com/posts/agentwright-starter

The last line of defence most AI apps forget: a monthly spend limit on the API provider's side.

It is the only limit that still works when your own metering code has a bug.

Connecting MCP servers to your own Claude agent loop: one env variable for all servers, stdio and HTTP, namespaced tool names, an allowlist.

Plus the detail that costs money: keep tool order stable or your prompt cache misses.

On our blog, link in profile.

How our blog publishes every day without a daily deploy: each post is uploaded ahead of time, and a small Cloudflare Pages middleware returns 404 until the post's date arrives in Asia/Seoul time.

One deploy per batch of eight posts, nothing to run each morning.

The catch with Claude prompt caching: the default cache lasts 5 minutes.

10,000-token prefix on Sonnet 5.5:
5-min write $0.025
1-hour write $0.04
read $0.001

One pause over 5 minutes and you write twice: $0.05. With the 1-hour cache: $0.041. Slow users need the 1-hour one.

We made a free remote MCP server for Claude API pricing.

Add https://agentwright.app/mcp to Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor and ask "what does this workload cost on Sonnet vs Haiku?" It knows caching and Batch API prices.

No sign-up, no key. Source is public.

Our Claude starter kit's agent loop is now public in full: 104 lines of TypeScript.

Streaming, parallel tool calls, a 12-turn limit, one cache breakpoint on the system prompt, and a plan-cap check before every model turn.

Read it before you write your own. Link in profile.

Not every Claude call has a user waiting: nightly digests, tagging, evals, backfills.

Send those through the Message Batches API and they cost half the standard price. Most batches finish within an hour; requests not done in 24 hours expire.

We ran our Polar billing code in Polar's sandbox with real signed webhooks. The purchase events arrived out of order: subscription.updated before subscription.created.

The plan stayed right: an older event never overwrites a newer one, and every delivery recomputes the plan.

A 2M-token monthly cap can cost you $0.20 (all cache reads on Sonnet) or $40 (all output on Opus).

Cap each user's spend in dollars, not tokens, and reserve the worst case before the request so two parallel calls can't slip past.

Code on our blog, link in profile.

Reading the same 20,000 tokens of context on Opus 5.5:

uncached: $0.08
from cache: $0.004

That 20x gap is why how you split work between agents shows up on the bill. A helper that shares the main agent's exact prefix pays the cache price. One with its own prompt starts cold.

Each usage row in our Claude kit stores raw token counts, the cost in integer micro-dollars and the price row id.

Haiku 5.5, 3,000 tokens in, 400 tokens out: 500 micro-dollars ($0.0005).

A price change is a new row. Past totals don't move, and every charge can be explained.

A SaaS boilerplate gives you sign-in, payments and a landing page.

A product where an agent does the work needs more, because every request costs you money:

- a tool loop with a turn limit
- a usage row per model call, per user
- plan caps checked before the call
- evals in CI

Three days of posting from a brand-new X account that started with 0 followers. Real numbers:

7 timeline posts: 9 impressions each on average
2 posts in X Communities: 46 and 13
Likes: 0

Small numbers, but communities are how a new account gets read by non-followers.

We opened sales for Agentwright Starter this week: the Next.js codebase behind the posts on this account, with metering, billing, auth and the agent loop already wired.

If you build on the Claude API, we'd like to hear what a kit like this is still missing. Link in profile.

A Claude agent loop sends its prefix again on every turn. 8,000 tokens of system prompt and tools, 10 turns on Sonnet 5.5:

no cache: $0.16
with cache: $0.027 (one write, nine reads)

That is the prefix alone. Put the cache breakpoint after the tools and keep their order fixed.

Per-user cost tracking for a Claude agent is less code than it sounds.

Every API response reports four token counts: input, output, cache write, cache read. Store one row per model call with the user id, the model and those four numbers.

Cost is then four multiplications.

10,000 document summaries, 2,000 tokens in and 300 out each:

Sonnet 5.5: $70
Sonnet 5.5, Batch API: $35
Haiku 5.5: $3.50
Haiku 5.5, Batch API: $1.75

For background work the model choice moves the bill 20x. Batching then halves what is left.

Claude Haiku 5.5 bills a prompt over 100,000 tokens at long-prompt prices, for the whole request.

99,000 tokens in, 1,000 out: $0.0104
101,000 tokens in, 1,000 out: $0.053

2% more context, 5x the cost. If your retrieval step can overshoot, cap it below the line.

Before a Claude call, reserve the worst case against the user's budget: max_tokens times the output price.

max_tokens 4,096:
Opus 5.5: $0.082
Sonnet 5.5: $0.041
Haiku 5.5: $0.002

Settle to real usage after the response. Lower max_tokens, more parallel calls under a cap.

How our posts go out at night with nobody awake: a JSON queue in the repo and a Cloudflare cron Worker that runs at :07 every hour and posts the next due item, one per run.

Before any queue change, a script checks real posting times, length, quiet hours and links.

Selling an agent by usage? Find the cost floor of one task first.

Sonnet 5.5, 6 turns, 30,000 input tokens in total with 80% read from cache, 3,000 output tokens:

input $0.012
cache reads $0.0024
output $0.03

About $0.044 a task. At $0.10 a task the margin is 56%.

A turn limit is also a spend limit.

Worst case for the output of one agent run, 12 turns at max_tokens 4,096:

Opus 5.5: $0.98
Sonnet 5.5: $0.49
Haiku 5.5: $0.025

Without a turn limit a run has no worst case, and nothing to check against a user's budget before it starts.

Every turn of an agent conversation sends the whole history again.

Opus 5.5, input per turn:
400,000 tokens: $1.60, or $0.08 read from cache
40,000 after compaction: $0.16, or $0.008 from cache

Caching cuts the price per token. Compaction cuts the tokens. You want both.

Our recent posts as a 2-follower account, by where they went:

shared into a community: 13 to 41 views each
timeline only: most got 0 to 4

With no audience yet, the timeline reaches almost nobody. So we write for the communities first and make each post useful on its own.

Magic-link sign-in breaks in a way testing won't show: corporate mail scanners open every link in the email, the token is used up, the real click fails.

The fix: link to your own page with a button, and let the button go to the real callback.

On our blog, link in profile.

A 200 from the Claude API is not always a finished answer. Check stop_reason first.

If it says max_tokens, the response was cut off, and the last tool call can be incomplete. Don't run a tool on input that was truncated; raise max_tokens or retry.

Price per token is the number people compare. Cost per finished task is the one you pay.

Opus 5.5, 20,000 tokens in, 2,000 out:
no cache: $0.12
18,000 of the input read from cache: $0.052

Same model, less than half the cost. Measure cost per task from your usage table.

A Next.js agent app on Vercel and Neon:

- pooled connection string in the app, direct string for migrations
- migrations outside the build
- enough function time for long agent turns
- functions near the database
- a DB branch per preview

On our blog, link in profile.

Several workers, one Postgres jobs table, no job taken twice: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

Add a lease (locked_until) when a worker claims a job. If the worker crashes, the lease runs out and another worker picks the job up again. No extra queue service.

Claude's token counting endpoint is free and takes the same input as a real request.

Use it to reject an oversized upload, price a large request, or route by size. Inside an agent loop, the previous response's usage is usually the better estimate.

On our blog, link in profile.

The Anthropic TypeScript SDK already retries 429, 5xx and connection errors for you, with backoff.

It cannot know whether the tool that ran before the failure already sent an email or charged a card. Store each tool result before the next model call, and never run it twice.

Long Claude agent conversations get expensive. Two ways to keep them small:

- context editing: clear old tool results
- compaction: replace old turns with a summary at a token threshold

How each one interacts with prompt caching and billing. On our blog, link in profile.

Most agent bugs that look like model mistakes are tool definition mistakes.

- the description says when to call the tool, not only what it does
- enums instead of free strings
- error messages that tell the model how to fix the call

How to write tool definitions Claude uses correctly: a verb-and-object name, a description that says when to call it, a schema that rules out wrong inputs, short results, and errors that lead to a correct retry.

Before/after examples in TypeScript. On our blog, link in profile.

The risky combination in an agent: it can read private data, it reads text written by someone else (web pages, emails, documents), and it can send data out.

A better system prompt doesn't fix that. Take one of the three away for each run, in code.

Prompt injection in a Claude agent with tools: a threat model, and the defences that hold in code.

Capabilities decided per run, authorization outside the model, closed exfiltration paths, and approval for side effects.

On our blog, link in profile.

Pick an agent's model by cost per passed task, not per token.

Replay 50 real tasks, check each result, divide spend by passes. At 40k in / 4k out:
- Opus 5.5: $0.24 a run, say 45 pass: $0.27 each
- Sonnet 5.5: $0.12 a run, say 30 pass: $0.20 each

Then price the 20 failures.

Letting users approve an agent's risky actions before they run: stop the loop on a gated tool call, store the pending action, show the exact arguments, execute once, then resume with the right tool_result.

Parallel calls and denials included. On our blog, link in profile.

Fable 5.2 as the planner, a cheaper model as the worker. One task at list prices:
planner 20k in / 2k out, 10 worker calls of 15k in / 1.5k out.

- all Fable 5.2: $2.04
- Sonnet 5.5 workers: $0.69
- Haiku 5.5 workers: $0.26

Most of the bill is the workers. Test them first.

WHERE user_id = $1 is one lock. Postgres row-level security is a second one, for the day a query or an agent tool forgets it.

Policies, a non-owner app role, set_config inside a transaction, poolers, and what to test. On our blog, link in profile.

Testing an agent tool is ordinary unit testing: a tool is a function.

For the loop, use a scripted fake client that returns a tool_use block and then end_turn. Fast, free, deterministic. Keep the checks that need the real model in a separate eval suite.

Tests for a Claude agent that never call Claude:

- tools as plain functions
- input schema tests
- a scripted fake client for the loop: tool_use / tool_result handling, errors, turn limits

Real-model checks stay in evals. On our blog, link in profile.

Postgres row-level security has a catch: the table owner skips the policies unless you add FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and superusers always skip them.

Connect the app as a separate role that does not own the tables, or the policies do nothing.

One request through a Claude agent SaaS, in order:

who is this, too many requests, budget left, which model, the tool loop, streaming, recording the cost, storing the conversation.

One map, with a detailed post for each step. On our blog, link in profile.

Schema-valid JSON from Claude is not the same as a correct answer.

Check stop_reason before you parse: max_tokens can cut the JSON off, and a refusal may not follow your schema. And a valid category can still be the wrong one. That part needs evals.

A Stop button for a Claude agent: pass the request's abort signal to the SDK and to your tools.

The tokens of a request that already started are still billed, so record the usage even when the stream ends early, and leave the conversation valid. On our blog, link in profile.

Store the Anthropic request id on every model call you log. The TypeScript SDK exposes it on the returned message as _request_id.

If you ever ask Anthropic support about one failed call, that id is the first thing they ask for.

Three cheap alerts before an AI bill surprises you, all from your own usage table:

- daily total against a budget
- one user far above their own normal
- burn rate in the last hour

Plus the provider-side spending limit as the last net. On our blog, link in profile.

Message Batches API results come back in any order.

Use your own job row's id as the custom_id, and match each result by it. Never rely on position. Results stay available for 29 days.

Five onboarding emails worth sending in an AI SaaS, each triggered by what the user did: welcome, first-success nudge, 80% of the plan used, limit reached, a quiet check-in.

A Postgres jobs table instead of a drip tool. On our blog, link in profile.

Before you add a vector database, give your agent a search tool on plain Postgres full-text search: a generated tsvector column, a GIN index, websearch_to_tsquery for model-written queries, short ranked results.

On our blog, link in profile.

Tracing Claude agent runs without an observability vendor: one row per run, one per step (model call or tool call), with timings, tokens, stop reasons and errors.

Then p95 latency, slow tools and failing tools are a SQL query each. On our blog, link in profile.

Use websearch_to_tsquery, not to_tsquery, when an agent writes the search query.

It accepts quotes, or, and a leading minus, and it never throws a syntax error. to_tsquery raises an error on bad syntax, and model-written queries will hit it.

Claude calls that nobody waits for (nightly digests, tagging, backfills) cost half the standard price through the Message Batches API.

A Postgres table to track them, a cron job that submits and collects, and per-user metering. On our blog, link in profile.

Combining keyword and vector search results: reciprocal rank fusion.

score = 1/(60 + keyword rank) + 1/(60 + vector rank)

It uses ranks only, so you never have to make ts_rank and cosine distance comparable. One SQL query does both.

Adding pgvector to an agent's Postgres search tool: an embedding column next to the tsvector, an HNSW index, keyword and vector results combined in one query, embeddings kept in sync.

And a small test set to prove it helped. On our blog, link in profile.

A user who uploads one PDF and asks five questions about it: with base64 you send the whole file five times.

Upload it once with the Files API and send the file id instead. Then keep a table of which user owns which file id.

PDF uploads in a Claude agent SaaS: base64 or the Files API, the request and page limits for your upload form, estimating the token cost before you send, and file ids scoped per user.

On our blog, link in profile.

Onboarding mail rule: check the condition when the mail is sent, not when it was scheduled.

A day-3 "try your first task" nudge must not go to someone who already did it on day 1.

A double click, a mobile retry or a reconnecting stream can start the same Claude agent run twice, and you pay twice.

A client-generated idempotency key, a unique constraint in Postgres, and a path that replays the stored answer. On our blog, link in profile.

Prompt injection defence that does not depend on the model: the agent never decides who the user is.

Tools take the user id from the server session, never from a tool argument. The model can be fooled; your authorization check can't.

Claude's web search server tool costs $10 per 1,000 searches, on top of tokens.

Set max_uses, use domain filters where you can, read the citations, and meter searches per user like tokens. On our blog, link in profile.

Store Claude agent conversations as content blocks (text, tool calls, tool results, thinking), and append only.

Editing earlier turns breaks prompt caching and can return 400s on current models. On our blog, link in profile.

Export my data, delete my account: in an AI product, user data also lives in uploaded files at Anthropic, your email provider, your payment provider and your logs.

Start with one written map of where data lives, and a test that keeps it honest. On our blog, link in profile.

Kill switches for an agent are worth having before the first incident:

- turn off one tool
- move a route to another model
- pause one user

A config table with a short cache changes them in seconds, without a deploy.

Kill switches for an AI agent: one runtime config table to disable a broken tool, switch a model, lower limits or pause an abusive user in seconds.

With a short cache, an audit log, safe defaults and the incident runbook. On our blog, link in profile.
